beats.narration: Begin by framing Foundations of Algorithm Analysis as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: A sorting algorithm must guarantee that the output list contains all input elements in non-decreasing order. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Foundations of Algorithm Analysis
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a side-by-side comparison of a problem statement and its corresponding resource bounds, highlighting the connection between specification and analysis.

beats.narration: Now define Asymptotic Notation Basics precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. Consider this worked case: Big-O notation captures the worst-case growth rate of an algorithm's time complexity as input size increases. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation Basics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a graph plotting input size against resource usage, with asymptotic curves labeled to illustrate growth rates.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Loop Invariants for Correctness operates in a concrete sequence. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Consider this worked case: In a search loop, the invariant states that the target element, if present, must reside in the unexamined portion of the array. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Loop Invariants for Correctness
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a loop structure with callouts marking the initialization step, the maintenance condition, and the termination check.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Divide-and-Conquer Strategy and make the decision criteria explicit. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Consider this worked case: Merge sort divides an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves into a single sorted array. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Animate a recursive tree structure where each node splits into two subproblems, then merges back up to show the combined result.

beats.narration: Apply Recurrence Relations to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort by accounting for splitting and merging costs. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Recurrence Relations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a recurrence equation alongside a step-by-step expansion showing how subproblem costs accumulate to the total cost.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Graph Algorithms Overview, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Consider this worked case: Breadth-first search traverses a graph level by level to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms Overview
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a graph with vertices and edges, highlighting the traversal order and marking visited nodes to demonstrate reachability and pathfinding.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Dynamic Programming Fundamentals with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Consider this worked case: The Fibonacci sequence can be computed efficiently by storing previously calculated values to avoid redundant recursive calls. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Dynamic Programming Fundamentals
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a table filling process where each cell references previously computed values, emphasizing the reuse of subproblem solutions.

beats.narration: Use Core Methods and Data Structures to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. Consider this worked case: Hash tables map keys to locations using a collision strategy to enable fast key-value lookups. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Core Methods and Data Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a hash table with keys, hash functions, and collision resolution paths, illustrating how mappings are stored and retrieved.

beats.narration: Connect Automata and Formal Languages to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Consider this worked case: A finite automaton accepts a string if its state transitions follow a defined sequence of symbols leading to an accepting state. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Automata and Formal Languages
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a state diagram with transitions labeled by input symbols, showing which paths lead to an accepting state and which do not.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space. Consider this worked case: Before implementing an algorithm, verify that the input/output contract is clear, the correctness proof holds, and the resource bounds are documented. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a checklist graphic with three boxes labeled 'Input/Output Contract', 'Correctness Proof', and 'Resource Bounds', each with a checkbox for verification.

sources.excerpt: This course provides a challenging introduction to the theory of computation with an emphasis on problem solving. Topics include formal languages, grammars, auto-mata theory, computability, and complexity. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-141 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-123 or SWEN-124 or CSECI-123 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-123 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

sources.author: OpenDSA Project
sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
